newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: UK's Blair warns against excessive labour laws.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair warns against excessive labour laws.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair told Europe's centre-left leaders on Friday that the best way of helping people into work was through education and not through more labour market regulations.

And, in a warning to the left-wing of his own Labour party, Blair said there would be no rolling back of the labour market reforms pushed through in the 18 years of Conservative rule he is fighting to end.

In a speech in Amsterdam, Blair repeated his pledge to take Britain into the European Union's Social Chapter -- designed to harmonise labour laws across the 15-member bloc -- and to introduce a national minimum wage.

But he told a conference on social policy: "Outside of those minimum standards of fairness, we need to encourage mobility, flexibility and employability. An over-rigid labour market in the end helps no-one...

"Of course there is a balance to be struck. But I say to those of my colleagues on the centre-left: let us be champions of fair but flexible labour markets... Otherwise we will find, as with the tax-and-spend debate, we just yield territory to the right who would abandon all forms of fairness."
Blair, less than four months away from an election which polls tip him to win, has dragged his party from the left to the centre of British politics.
But Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservatives accuse him of failing to quell Labour's old-style socialist tax and spend instincts.

Blair used Friday's conference -- attended by Dutch Labour premier Wim Kok, as well as Spain's former socialist leader Felipe Gonzalez and former European Commission President Jacques Delors -- to lay out his blueprint for welfare reform.
"It is our task to create a genuine "one nation' society," said Blair, in a deliberate echo of Major's 1992 election campaign pledge of a "classless society".

But Blair warned: "There will be no option of a life permanently on full benefit. Where there is a suitable offer, people will be expected to take this up. That is fair. Rights and responsibilities go together."
Blair's "tough love" approach has angered some on the left of his party.
But it has won back voters who quit the Labour party under the influence of former prime minister Margaret Thatcher's crusading zeal.
Blair fleshed out his speech with proposals aimed at getting Britain's one million unemployed lone parents back to work.

His plans include job counselling, better child-care provision such as after-school clubs funded from National Lottery money, and the use of technology like 24-hour telephone banking to offer people fast and flexible access to government services like employment centres.
Conservative Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley has atacked Blair's plans as a poor imitation of the government's ideas with the added disadvantage of higher cost.
But Blair said all his schemes would be within existing budgets and could save money.
